title: Meditation, understanding, strength, food, water (7.6–7.10)
hook: the ladder climbs past thought to meditation, and then takes a surprising turn: toward strength, food and rain

segments.voice: Yesterday: name, the first rung, then speech, mind, will and thought. Your line was each is greater.

Draw a spiritual ladder, and you'd probably make it climb from the body toward the mind: earthy things at the bottom, airy things at the top. Sanatkumara's ladder starts that way. Name, speech, mind, will, thought, each more inward. Today it reaches meditation, the most inward step yet. And right after that, it does something nobody expects. It climbs toward a strong arm, a meal, and a rain cloud.
screen: `A LADDER FROM BODY TO MIND.` → `TODAY: MEDITATION.` → `THEN A STRONG ARM, A MEAL, A RAIN CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Greater than thought, Sanatkumara says, is meditation, dhyana. The earth meditates, as it were. The sky meditates, as it were. The waters, the mountains, gods and people, all meditate, as it were. Think of a mountain at dusk, utterly still. People who achieve greatness, he adds, seem to have a share of it, while small-minded people are quarrelsome and gossiping. Greater than meditation is understanding, vijnana: by it one knows the Vedas, right and wrong, this world and the next. Then the turn. Greater than understanding is strength. One strong person can make a hundred people of understanding tremble. The earth stands by strength; the mountains stand by it. Greater than strength is food. Go without eating for ten days, and even if you live, you can't see or hear or think or understand. Remember Shvetaketu's fast? Same point. Food returns, and so do they. Greater than food is water. When the rains fail, people grow sick with worry about food; when the rains are good, they're glad. The earth, the sky, the mountains, people, animals, grass and trees, he says, are all water in solid form. So why does the ladder climb into the body? One way to read it: Sanatkumara isn't ranking spirit over matter. He's asking what each thing depends on. Understanding on strength; strength on food; food on rain. The ladder climbs by asking what holds this up.
screen: `THE EARTH MEDITATES, AS IT WERE.` · `UNDERSTANDING, THEN STRENGTH.` · `TEN DAYS WITHOUT FOOD.` · `EARTH AND MOUNTAINS: WATER, MADE SOLID.` · then, large: `WHAT HOLDS THIS UP?`

segments.voice: Let your body settle like rock, heavy and still, held by the ground; a mountain doesn't try. Let the breath move like weather over a peak and thoughts pass like clouds, and just sit, as the earth and the sky and the waters sit, meditating, as it were.
Meditation. Dhyana, the rung above thought: the stillness of earth, sky and mountains. Above it, understanding, strength, food and water.
Your line: the ladder climbs. Tomorrow, the top of it. Day three hundred fifty-four, done.

howItsDone: Dhyana, meditation, is practiced across Hindu traditions, from Vedanta to yoga, where it is the seventh limb of Patanjali's eight; teachers often describe it with images of stillness like a mountain or a lamp in a windless place.

chat.says: Why does Sanatkumara's ladder go from meditation up to food and water?
options: It asks what holds each up: understanding needs strength, strength food, food rain.
It shows that the body matters more than the mind or the spirit.
It's a warning that meditating is useless unless you've eaten well first.
